segments: ...a village, their leader Ali.
And he shed much blood of the Arabs;
and they ruled over all the cities of the south and parts of Syria and Sinjar for many years.
And al-Muhtadi himself expelled the male and female singers from Samarra,
where their kings were residing at this time,
and he broke the musical instruments.
And he killed the lions, leopards, and dogs with which the kings before him used to play.
And against him, again, the Turkish slaves arose and killed him.
For he fled before them while riding a horse and crying out:
"O people,
help your king!"
And no one answered him.
And when he entered a certain courtyard,
the Turks entered after him.
He, however, fled from roof to roof;
and thus he was overtaken and killed in the year 256
— 256 of the Arabs.
At this time, Hunayn the excellent physician, the son of Ishaq, was renowned,
whose father was an apothecary from the city of Hira.
And he loved to learn medicine,
and he entered Baghdad,
and began to study the Alexandrian Compendium under the physician Yuhanna ibn Masawayh.
And one day, when he repeated a question to Yuhanna,
the latter became angry, expelled him, and said to him:
"What do you have to do with medicine? Those like you should sell small coins on the street!"
And the young Hunayn was deeply grieved,
and he went out weeping,
and went to the land of the Romans.
And he was there until he had learned the Greek language thoroughly,
and gained the ability to translate books from Greek into Syriac,
and from Syriac into Arabic.
And he returned again to Baghdad in Greek attire,
and went to Gabriel, the chief physician, the son of Bukhtishu.
And when he tested his knowledge,
he honored him greatly,
and called him "Rabban Hunayn."
And he said to those present:
"If this youth lives,
he will leave no memory of Sergius of Resh'aina."
And the news of him reached Yuhanna who had expelled him,
and he brought him to himself,
and asked him for forgiveness.
And thus, day by day his distinction increased.
And he began to translate various kinds of learning,
until he died in the month of (at the beginning of) the First Kanun in the year 1188
— 1188 of the Greeks
(876 of our Lord),
which is the year 260
— 260 of the Arabs.
And he left two sons,
Ishaq and David.
